cards.heading: Feasibility analysis vs. the business plan
cards.body:
**Feasibility analysis** is a structured assessment of whether a business idea can realistically be built, sold, financed, and operated by the team pursuing it, given the resources and constraints they actually have. It asks "Can we?" A business plan asks a completely different question — "How will we?" — and only makes sense to write AFTER feasibility confirms the venture is actually viable.

Feasibility analysis is concise: a structured assessment across four dimensions, producing a go/no-go/pivot decision. A business plan is the full document — strategy, marketing, operations, financials — a roadmap for execution.

Why the order matters: writing the full business plan before feasibility analysis risks investing days or weeks of detailed planning into a venture that turns out to be fundamentally unviable.

cards.heading: The four dimensions of feasibility
cards.body:
Every venture gets tested across exactly four dimensions:

1. Technical — can the product actually be built?
2. Market — will people actually want it and pay for it?
3. Financial — can the venture actually sustain itself?
4. Organisational — can THIS SPECIFIC team actually execute it?

Notice the last one: feasibility isn't just "is this a good idea in general" — it's whether this particular team, with its particular skills, resources, and constraints, can pull it off. A brilliant idea can still be infeasible for a specific team, right now, even if it would be perfectly feasible for a different team with different resources.

cards.heading: Technical feasibility: can it be built?
cards.body:
Five questions: is the tech stack suitable and within the team's actual skill set? Should components be built in-house or bought/integrated? How complex are the required third-party integrations? Will the architecture scale if users grow quickly? What data security and privacy requirements apply?

**Build vs. buy**: integrating proven infrastructure (payments, authentication, messaging) frees scarce engineering time for what's actually unique — the core value proposition. Example: a B2B invoicing tool integrates an existing payment API (buy) and directs all its own engineering effort toward its unique invoice-generation and approval-workflow features (build).

Risk classification: HIGH (cutting-edge or unproven tech, or skills the team lacks), MEDIUM (proven tech combined in a new or complex way), LOW (well-understood tech in a domain the team already knows well).

cards.heading: The MVP as a feasibility tool, not just a launch plan
cards.body:
An MVP (Minimum Viable Product) is the smallest version of a product that still tests its core value proposition with real users — not a prototype, not a demo, but a real, if limited, product real users can actually use.

The MVP question: what is the single most important assumption about our product that we need to test, and what is the smallest thing we could build to test it? Include the core value proposition. Exclude every secondary and tertiary feature, no matter how tempting.

A tight MVP scope does three things at once: reduces technical risk, shortens the time to real-user feedback, and avoids months spent building features nobody actually asked for.

cards.heading: Market feasibility: four indicators, a stricter lens
cards.body:
This re-examines Week 2's opportunity-validation work with a stricter, go/no-go lens:

• Problem confirmed real — multiple independent sources (interviews, observed behaviour, data) point to the same pain point, unprompted, not just one enthusiastic conversation
• Market is reachable — the team has a specific, plausible plan to actually find and communicate with target customers, not just a hope that they'll show up
• Customers will switch — dissatisfaction with current alternatives is strong enough to actually motivate real behaviour change, not just mild annoyance
• Timing is right — a credible "why now": something specific has genuinely changed (technology, regulation, behaviour)

Passing Week 2's validation doesn't automatically mean passing this stricter re-check — this is where a team honestly re-examines its own optimism.

cards.heading: Financial feasibility: costs and break-even
cards.body:
Cost categories: development (MVP build, design, licences), hosting and infrastructure (cloud, APIs, storage), marketing and acquisition (ads, content), salaries and contractor payments, legal and administrative (registration, compliance).

Basic revenue: price per customer per month × number of paying customers.

**Break-even point**: fixed costs ÷ (revenue per customer − variable cost per customer). This tells you exactly how many paying customers you need before the venture stops losing money on operations.

**Runway**: the length of time a venture can keep operating before running out of money — current cash ÷ monthly net spend (burn rate). Sound long-term economics can still fail if the runway runs out before break-even is actually reached — being right eventually doesn't help if the money is gone first.

cards.heading: Break-even in practice: Amaka's numbers, tested harder
cards.body:
Remember Amaka's inventory-tracking SaaS from Week 2? Fixed monthly costs ₦300,000, price ₦1,500 per shop, variable cost ₦200 per shop. Break-even = ₦300,000 ÷ (₦1,500 − ₦200) = ₦300,000 ÷ ₦1,300 ≈ 231 paying shops needed.

But Week 2's own SOM estimate for year one was only 120 shops. 120 is less than 231 — a clear financial feasibility WARNING. Her venture wasn't a bad idea; it just doesn't yet balance at the numbers she started with.

Responses worth testing: raise the price to ₦2,000/shop (new break-even ≈ 167 shops — much closer), reduce fixed costs, or set a more aggressive, evidence-justified customer-acquisition target. This is exactly why feasibility analysis happens BEFORE the business plan — catching this now costs an afternoon of recalculating; catching it after launch costs real money already spent.

cards.heading: Organisational feasibility: can THIS team execute?
cards.body:
Four questions: does the team have the technical skills to build the MVP, or a credible plan to acquire them? Does the team have relevant experience or founder-market fit in this specific problem space? What physical and digital resources are required, and are they realistically accessible? Is the team's current time and energy capacity realistic given other commitments (a full course load, a job, family responsibilities)?

Closing a skill or resource gap has three honest paths: **Learning** (a founder invests time acquiring the skill — works when the gap is narrow), **Recruiting** (add a co-founder or hire with the missing skill — for large or urgent gaps), **Advising** (a mentor or advisor fills the gap without taking equity or salary).

The rule that matters most: name every gap honestly, early. A gap that's named can be planned around; a gap that's quietly ignored eventually becomes the reason the venture stalls.

cards.heading: The feasibility matrix, and the go/pivot/no-go call
cards.body:
Score all four dimensions — technical, market, financial, organisational — from 1 (very weak evidence) to 5 (strong, well-evidenced), each with a written one- or two-sentence justification, not a gut-feeling number.

GO — all four dimensions show credible, evidence-backed feasibility: proceed to the full business plan.
**PIVOT** — a serious weakness exists in one dimension, but the underlying problem and team remain promising: adjust the specific weak point and re-test, don't abandon the whole venture.
**NO-GO** — fundamental, unresolvable weaknesses show up across MULTIPLE dimensions at once: abandon this particular idea and look elsewhere.

Amaka's venture, with its break-even gap, is a textbook PIVOT case: one real financial weakness, everything else intact — worth adjusting price or acquisition targets and re-testing, not worth abandoning outright.

It's not that the idea is bad — Amaka's numbers just need adjusting, and that's exactly what a PIVOT verdict means: no wahala, tweak the price, no need to scrap the whole hustle.

quiz.question: What is the key difference in the question each of these asks: feasibility analysis vs. a full business plan?
options: They ask exactly the same question in different formats
Feasibility analysis asks 'Can we?'; a business plan asks 'How will we?' — and the plan should only be written after feasibility confirms viability
A business plan always comes first, feasibility analysis comes after
Feasibility analysis is only used by investors, never by the founding team
quiz.explanation: Feasibility analysis is the concise, earlier 'can this actually work?' check; the business plan is the fuller execution roadmap that only makes sense to write once feasibility has confirmed the venture is viable — writing the plan first risks wasted effort on an unviable idea.

quiz.question: Why does organisational feasibility specifically ask whether THIS team can execute, rather than just whether the idea is good?
options: Because a good idea can still be infeasible for a specific team's actual skills, resources, and constraints, even if it would be feasible for a different team
Because organisational feasibility is really about the idea's originality
Because only investors care about the founding team
Because team composition never actually affects whether a venture succeeds
quiz.explanation: Feasibility isn't a generic judgement of the idea — it's specifically about whether THIS team, with its particular skills and resources right now, can realistically pull it off, which is exactly why organisational feasibility is its own separate dimension.

quiz.question: In the build-vs-buy decision for technical feasibility, why would a B2B invoicing tool integrate an existing payment API rather than build its own payment processing?
options: Building payment processing in-house is always illegal
It frees scarce engineering capacity for what's actually unique to the product — its invoice-generation and approval-workflow features
Payment APIs are always free to use
Customers refuse to trust integrated payment APIs
quiz.explanation: Integrating proven infrastructure like payments lets the team focus limited engineering time on their actual unique value proposition, rather than reinventing a solved problem — that's the core logic of build vs. buy.

quiz.question: Using Amaka's numbers (fixed costs ₦300,000/month, price ₦1,500/shop, variable cost ₦200/shop), approximately how many paying shops does she need to break even?
options: 120 shops
167 shops
231 shops
300 shops
quiz.explanation: ₦300,000 ÷ (₦1,500 − ₦200) = ₦300,000 ÷ ₦1,300 ≈ 231 shops — well above her Week 2 SOM estimate of 120 shops, which is exactly the financial feasibility warning this chapter highlights.

quiz.question: Amaka's break-even is 231 shops but her realistic Year 1 SOM is only 120 shops. According to the go/pivot/no-go framework, what does this situation call for?
options: An automatic NO-GO, since the numbers don't currently work
A PIVOT — one real financial weakness with everything else intact, worth adjusting (price, costs, or acquisition target) and re-testing
A GO, since the idea itself is still good
Ignoring the gap and proceeding to the full business plan anyway
quiz.explanation: PIVOT — a serious weakness in one dimension (financial) with the underlying problem and team still promising calls for adjusting the specific weak point (e.g. raising price to ₦2,000, cutting fixed costs) and re-testing, not abandoning the whole venture.

quiz.question: According to the organisational feasibility framework, what is the correct response to a founding team having a large, urgent skill gap (e.g. no one who can build the required tech)?
options: Ignore it and hope it resolves itself
Recruiting — add a co-founder or hire with the missing skill, since learning is realistically too slow for a large or urgent gap
Abandon the venture immediately
Wait until after launch to address it
quiz.explanation: Of the three gap-closing paths (Learning, Recruiting, Advising), Recruiting is specifically for large or urgent gaps — Learning works when the gap is narrow enough for a founder to close it themselves in reasonable time.

theory.question: Explain why feasibility analysis is deliberately done BEFORE writing a full business plan, and use Amaka's break-even gap (120 SOM vs. ~231 break-even) to illustrate what could go wrong if the order were reversed.
theory.modelAnswer: Feasibility analysis asks the concise question 'can this venture realistically be built, sold, financed, and operated by this team?' across four dimensions, producing a fast go, pivot, or no-go decision. A full business plan asks a much bigger question, 'how will we execute this?', requiring days or weeks of detailed work across strategy, marketing, operations, and financials. Doing feasibility first means catching fundamental problems cheaply, before investing that larger effort. In Amaka's case, her Week 2 opportunity looked promising with a SOM of 120 shops in year one, but Week 4's financial feasibility check reveals she actually needs about 231 paying shops just to break even at her original pricing — nearly double her realistic year-one customer count. Catching this now costs an afternoon of recalculating numbers and considering a price increase or cost reduction. If she had skipped feasibility analysis and gone straight to writing a full business plan and building the product, she could have spent weeks or months of real effort and money before discovering the same fundamental gap — at which point it's far more costly and disruptive to fix.
keyPoints: Feasibility analysis: fast, structured 'can we?' check across 4 dimensions
Business plan: much larger 'how will we?' effort, only worth doing after feasibility passes
Amaka's break-even (~231 shops) exceeds her Week 2 SOM (120 shops) — a real financial gap
Catching this in feasibility analysis is cheap; catching it after building/planning would be far costlier

theory.question: Describe the four dimensions of feasibility analysis, and explain using Amaka's situation why a venture can pass three dimensions strongly while still requiring a PIVOT rather than a GO.
theory.modelAnswer: The four dimensions are technical (can the product actually be built?), market (will people want it and pay for it?), financial (can the venture sustain itself?), and organisational (can this specific team execute it?). A GO decision requires all four dimensions to show credible, evidence-backed feasibility together — it isn't enough for most of them to look strong. In Amaka's case, her venture likely scores well on technical feasibility (inventory-tracking software isn't cutting-edge technology), market feasibility (Week 2's validation work confirmed a real, reachable problem), and possibly organisational feasibility (assuming she has or can acquire the needed skills). But her financial feasibility reveals a real weakness: her break-even point of roughly 231 shops exceeds her realistic year-one customer target of 120 shops. Because this is one serious weakness in an otherwise promising venture, rather than fundamental problems across multiple dimensions, the correct call is PIVOT — adjust the specific weak point (price, costs, or acquisition pace) and re-test — not NO-GO, which is reserved for unresolvable weaknesses spread across several dimensions at once.
keyPoints: Technical, Market, Financial, Organisational — all four required for a GO
Amaka likely scores well on technical/market/organisational feasibility
Financial feasibility is the one real weakness (break-even exceeds SOM)
One serious weakness + otherwise promising venture = PIVOT, not NO-GO

cards.heading: Strategy is the answer to 'how will we win?'
cards.body:
Business strategy is a deliberate set of choices about where a company will compete, how it'll serve customers better than the alternatives, and how it'll sustain that advantage over time. Porter's three generic strategies — pursuing all three at once without a deliberate choice just leaves a venture "stuck in the middle," good at nothing in particular:

• **Cost leadership** — the lowest cost structure in the market, enabling the lowest price at an acceptable margin. Example: a payroll app at ₦1,200/month against competitors charging ₦5,000-10,000, achieved through automation and self-serve onboarding.
• **Differentiation** — offer something customers genuinely value that competitors don't, and charge a premium for it. Example: a legal-document tool preloaded with actual Nigerian legal templates, built by practising lawyers.
• **Focus/niche** — concentrate all resources on one narrow segment and serve it exceptionally well. Example: payroll and compliance software built specifically for West African NGOs, nothing else.

cards.heading: Software-specific sources of sustainable advantage
cards.body:
Five ways a software venture keeps winning even after competitors notice it's working — and they often compound: a product with network effects that also creates switching costs becomes very hard to displace.

• **Network effects** — the product becomes more valuable to each user as more users join
• **Platform lock-in/switching costs** — time, data, and integrations invested make switching genuinely costly over time
• **Data advantage** — proprietary data improves personalisation and defaults new entrants simply can't match
• **Ecosystem & integrations** — deep ties to a customer's other tools create mutual dependency
• **Embedded domain expertise** — real insider industry knowledge built directly into workflows and templates

A good feature can be copied in weeks. A genuine network effect or years of accumulated customer data usually can't be.

cards.heading: Crafting a testable value proposition
cards.body:
A **value proposition** is a clear, specific statement of the benefit a product delivers to a defined customer segment, in a way that makes it preferable to the available alternatives. The formula: "For [target customer] who [specific problem], [product name] is a [category] that [key benefit], unlike [main alternative] which [specific shortfall]."

Applied to Amaka's venture — now officially named StockPilot: "For small retail shops in Nigerian cities who lose sales because they cannot track stock levels accurately, StockPilot is an inventory management app that sends automatic low-stock alerts and reorder reminders — unlike paper stock books and spreadsheets, which require manual counting and are frequently left unupdated."

Four common mistakes: a target customer that's too broad, a feature list instead of an actual benefit statement, no named alternative to compare against, and writing it in future tense ("will help" instead of "helps").

cards.heading: The Value Proposition Canvas
cards.body:
Splits into two matched halves. Customer Profile: Jobs (the tasks and goals customers are actually trying to accomplish), Pains (frustrations, risks, and obstacles they run into), Gains (positive outcomes and aspirations they have).

Value Map: Products & Services (what the venture actually offers), **Pain Relievers** (exactly how the product reduces each specific pain), **Gain Creators** (exactly how the product produces each specific gain).

"Fit" happens when the Value Map's strongest pain relievers and gain creators address the Customer Profile's MOST significant pains and gains — not every single one of them. StockPilot's job is "know what stock I have without counting it myself"; its pain reliever is the automatic low-stock alert; its gain creator is never losing a sale to an item that quietly ran out.

cards.heading: The ten sections of a software business plan
cards.body:
1. Executive Summary
2. Company Description
3. Market Analysis
4. Product/Service Description
5. Competitive Strategy & Value Proposition
6. Marketing & Sales Strategy
7. Operations Plan
8. Financial Plan
9. Risk Analysis
10. Appendices

Section 5 — the chosen strategy, primary advantage, and **value proposition** statement — is exactly what this week's work feeds directly into. Every section built across this course so far (opportunity, ownership, feasibility) has been quietly assembling the earlier sections of this exact document.

cards.heading: How different audiences read the same plan
cards.body:
The same ten-section document gets read completely differently depending on who's reading it — know your audience before you pitch:

• Investors (angels, VCs) — read the executive summary and team first; want to see a large market, real differentiation, a credible team, grounded projections
• Bank lenders — read cash-flow projections and collateral first; want stable revenue, documented assets, a clear repayment timeline
• Business partners — read the product description and traction first; want existing customers, a working product, an obvious **value proposition**
• Grant funders — read social/developmental impact first; want a clear need, a realistic budget, measurable outcomes
• The founding team itself — reads the operational and financial sections first; needs defined milestones, realistic assumptions, clear ownership

The same plan, five completely different first impressions — pitching a bank lender like an investor (or vice versa) wastes the exact page that would have convinced them.

quiz.question: A venture tries to be simultaneously the cheapest option, the most differentiated option, and the most niche-focused option, without committing to any one of Porter's strategies. What happens?
options: It automatically wins on all three fronts at once
It ends up 'stuck in the middle' — not clearly winning on any single dimension
This is actually the recommended approach for all software ventures
It becomes a monopoly by default
quiz.explanation: Porter's framework specifically warns that pursuing all three generic strategies at once, without a deliberate choice, leaves a venture 'stuck in the middle' — not genuinely competitive on cost, differentiation, or focus.

quiz.question: Why do network effects and data advantage count as particularly durable sources of competitive advantage, compared to a single new feature?
options: They're legally protected by patents automatically
A feature can typically be copied by a competitor in weeks; accumulated network effects or years of proprietary data are much harder to replicate quickly
They cost nothing to build
They only matter for hardware companies, not software
quiz.explanation: A feature is often copyable relatively quickly, but a genuine network effect (value that compounds with more users) or years of accumulated proprietary data takes real time to build and can't simply be copied overnight.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of the four common mistakes to avoid when writing a value proposition?
options: Naming a specific competing alternative
Writing it in present tense
Writing it as a feature list instead of an actual benefit statement
Defining a narrow target customer
quiz.explanation: A feature list instead of a benefit statement is one of the four common mistakes (alongside a target customer that's too broad, no named alternative, and writing in future tense) — a value proposition needs to state the BENEFIT, not just list features.

quiz.question: In the Value Proposition Canvas, StockPilot's automatic low-stock alert is best classified as which element?
options: A Job
A Pain
A Pain Reliever
A Gain
quiz.explanation: A Pain Reliever — it's part of the Value Map, describing exactly how the product reduces a specific pain (losing sales because stock levels aren't tracked), as distinct from the Customer Profile's Jobs/Pains/Gains.

quiz.question: A bank lender evaluating a software business plan will typically look FIRST at which section?
options: Executive summary and team
Cash-flow projections and collateral
Social/developmental impact
Product description and traction
quiz.explanation: Bank lenders read cash-flow projections and collateral first, wanting to see stable revenue, documented assets, and a clear repayment timeline — a different starting point than an investor (executive summary/team) or a grant funder (social impact).

quiz.question: Which strategy does 'payroll and compliance software built only for West African NGOs' best represent?
options: Cost leadership
Differentiation
Focus/niche
Product-led growth
quiz.explanation: Focus/niche — concentrating all resources on one narrow segment (West African NGOs specifically) and serving it exceptionally well, rather than trying to serve every organisation type or compete purely on price.

theory.question: Explain Porter's three generic strategies using the specific examples given in this chapter, and describe what 'stuck in the middle' means and why it's a dangerous position for a venture.
theory.modelAnswer: Porter's three generic strategies are cost leadership (the lowest cost structure enabling the lowest price at acceptable margin, like a payroll app at ₦1,200/month against competitors charging ₦5,000-10,000 through automation and self-serve onboarding), differentiation (offering something customers genuinely value that competitors don't, and charging a premium, like a legal-document tool preloaded with real Nigerian legal templates built by practising lawyers), and focus/niche (concentrating all resources on one narrow segment and serving it exceptionally well, like payroll software built only for West African NGOs). 'Stuck in the middle' describes a venture that tries to pursue all three at once without committing to any single one — it's not the cheapest option, not clearly differentiated, and not focused on any specific segment. This is dangerous because customers have no clear reason to choose it over a competitor that has made a deliberate strategic choice: a price-sensitive customer will pick the genuinely cheapest option, a customer wanting something unique will pick the genuinely differentiated option, and a venture 'stuck in the middle' loses both kinds of customer.
keyPoints: Cost leadership — lowest price via lowest cost structure
Differentiation — unique value, charged at a premium
Focus/niche — one narrow segment, served exceptionally well
'Stuck in the middle' = no deliberate choice = no clear reason for any customer to choose it

theory.question: Using StockPilot's value proposition as your example, explain the value proposition formula and describe two of the four common mistakes it deliberately avoids.
theory.modelAnswer: The value proposition formula is: 'For [target customer] who [specific problem], [product name] is a [category] that [key benefit], unlike [main alternative] which [specific shortfall].' StockPilot's version fills this in specifically: for small retail shops in Nigerian cities who lose sales because they cannot track stock levels accurately, StockPilot is an inventory management app that sends automatic low-stock alerts and reorder reminders, unlike paper stock books and spreadsheets, which require manual counting and are frequently left unupdated. This avoids the 'target customer too broad' mistake by naming a specific segment (small retail shops in Nigerian cities) rather than 'anyone who sells things.' It also avoids the 'feature list, not a benefit statement' mistake by stating the actual outcome (not losing sales, not having to manually count stock) rather than just listing features like 'has alerts and reminders' without explaining why that matters to the customer. It also names a specific alternative (paper stock books and spreadsheets) with its specific shortfall (requires manual counting, frequently left unupdated), avoiding the 'no named alternative' mistake, and is written in present tense ('sends,' not 'will send'), avoiding the future-tense mistake.
keyPoints: Formula: For [target customer] who [problem], [product] is a [category] that [benefit], unlike [alternative] which [shortfall]
Avoids 'too broad' by naming small retail shops specifically
Avoids 'feature list' by stating the benefit (not losing sales), not just features
Names a specific alternative and its shortfall; written in present tense

cards.heading: Marketing is the full customer lifecycle, not just ads
cards.body:
Advertising is one small tactic inside a much broader marketing function: identifying, reaching, converting, and retaining customers. The classic 4 Ps, applied specifically to software:

• Product — frequent updates, multiple versions, features that evolve with real user feedback
• Price — recurring subscription, tiered, usage-based, or freemium: a strategic choice, not an afterthought
• Place — digital distribution through app stores, the web, APIs, SaaS: global reach from day one, unlike a physical shop
• Promotion — content marketing, SEO, community, developer relations, product-led growth

**Product-led growth (PLG)** is when the product itself drives acquisition, conversion, and expansion — no separate sales team required to close every deal. Slack, Dropbox, Figma, and Notion all built their early growth this way: try the free version, get hooked, invite colleagues, someone upgrades.

cards.heading: Five pricing models for software
cards.body:
• **Freemium** — a free core tier, premium features paid; needs a large base since typical conversion is only 2-5%
• **Tiered** — Good/Better/Best; anchoring and decoy pricing nudge customers toward the higher tier
• Usage-based — pay per API call, message, or GB; aligns cost with value delivered, but needs accurate metering
• **Per-seat** — scales with active users; simple to explain, but can cap usage within an organisation
• **Enterprise/custom** — negotiated pricing with SLAs and compliance terms; longer sales cycle, but much larger deals

Costly mistake: underpricing out of fear. A price set too low doesn't just cost revenue — it signals low value and tends to attract the least loyal customers, the ones most likely to churn at the first better deal. Price relative to the value actually delivered, not to whatever feels comfortable to charge.

cards.heading: The acquisition funnel, and B2B vs. B2C
cards.body:
Every customer moves through the same five stages: Awareness → Interest → Consideration → Conversion → Retention. But HOW they move through it differs sharply by market:

• Decision-maker — a single individual user (B2C) vs. multiple stakeholders who all need convincing (B2B)
• Sales cycle — hours to days (B2C) vs. weeks to months (B2B)
• Deal size — small, scales through volume (B2C) vs. large per customer (B2B)
• Primary channels — app stores, social, SEO (B2C) vs. direct sales, LinkedIn, events (B2B)

Trying to sell StockPilot the way a B2C mobile game sells itself — pure app-store discovery, no direct outreach — would badly mismatch a market of small shop owners who need someone to actually explain and demonstrate the product first.

cards.heading: Churn: the leak nobody notices until it's huge
cards.body:
**Churn rate** is the percentage of customers who cancel or stop paying during a given period. Even a churn rate that sounds small compounds brutally over time: at 5% monthly churn, 200 customers in January shrink to only about 106 remaining by December (200 × 0.95¹²) — the venture has to acquire roughly 94 new customers over the year just to STAND STILL, before counting any actual growth.

This is exactly why retention gets called "the other half of marketing" — acquiring customers through a leaking bucket means running the acquisition machine flat-out just to stay in place, let alone grow.

cards.heading: Onboarding and customer success: the actual retention levers
cards.body:
**Onboarding** is the highest-leverage retention investment available. The goal: minimise "time to value" — the gap between sign-up and the customer's first genuinely meaningful success. It needs to be an active, guided process — not a welcome email, not a docs page nobody reads. Common failures: too much setup before any value appears, feature overload dumped on day one, and no context for what the customer was actually trying to accomplish in the first place.

**Customer success** means proactively monitoring usage for early warning signs of churn — declining activity, unused features, repeated support requests — and intervening BEFORE the customer actually leaves, not after. In an early-stage venture, this job usually falls directly on the founders themselves, since there's no dedicated team for it yet.

cards.heading: Unit economics: CAC, LTV, and the 3:1 benchmark
cards.body:
**CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost)** = total marketing & sales spend ÷ new customers acquired. **LTV (Lifetime Value)** = average monthly revenue per customer ÷ monthly churn rate. **Payback period** = CAC ÷ (monthly revenue − monthly variable cost); healthy target is 12 months or less.

StockPilot's own numbers: CAC = ₦800,000 ÷ 40 new customers = ₦20,000 per customer. LTV = ₦1,500 (her established monthly price) ÷ 0.05 churn rate = ₦30,000. LTV:CAC = 1.5:1.

The healthy benchmark is 3:1 or higher — spending ₦1 to earn back ₦3 or more over a customer's lifetime. At 1.5:1, StockPilot returns only 1.5× what it spends acquiring each customer — below benchmark, on top of the break-even gap already flagged in Week 4. Fixes: raise the price (which Week 4's pivot already pointed toward), reduce churn through better onboarding, or find a cheaper acquisition channel.

cards.heading: The 90-day go-to-market plan
cards.body:
Six components, no more: Target segment (the specific beachhead from Week 2 — not a broad market), Key message (the one thing the customer must understand, straight from this week's value proposition), Primary channels (one or two channels used exclusively for the first 90 days, not a scattered attempt at everything), First-customer target (a specific, realistic number of paying customers or active users), Specific actions (a week-by-week or month-by-month list of concrete activities), and Success metrics (2-3 numbers that actually indicate whether the plan is working).

Key metrics worth tracking: MRR, new customers per period, trial-to-paid conversion, CAC, LTV, monthly churn, NPS. StockPilot's own plan: target segment = small retail shops in her city (the exact Week 2 beachhead), key message = the low-stock-alert value proposition, primary channel = direct outreach to shop owners (matching B2B, not B2C, acquisition). The whole term paper now reads as one coherent argument, not six disconnected sections.

It signals low value and tends to attract the least loyal customers, who are the most likely to churn for a better deal
It has no real downside, since some revenue beats none
It automatically improves customer retention
quiz.explanation: Underpricing doesn't just leave revenue on the table — it signals low value and tends to attract price-sensitive customers with the least loyalty, exactly the customers most likely to leave the moment a cheaper alternative appears.

App stores don't allow B2B software of any kind
StockPilot has no target customer at all

theory.question: Explain the CAC and LTV formulas using StockPilot's actual numbers, and describe what the resulting 1.5:1 LTV:CAC ratio means for the venture's viability, including what could be done to fix it.
theory.modelAnswer: CAC (Customer Acquisition Cost) is total marketing and sales spend divided by new customers acquired; for StockPilot this is ₦800,000 spent to acquire 40 new customers, giving a CAC of ₦20,000 per customer. LTV (Lifetime Value) is average monthly revenue per customer divided by the monthly churn rate; for StockPilot this is ₦1,500 monthly revenue divided by a 5% (0.05) monthly churn rate, giving an LTV of ₦30,000. Dividing LTV by CAC gives the ratio: ₦30,000 ÷ ₦20,000 = 1.5:1. The healthy benchmark for this ratio is 3:1 or higher, meaning a venture should earn back at least three times what it spends acquiring each customer over that customer's lifetime. At only 1.5:1, StockPilot is currently earning back just 1.5 times its acquisition cost, well below a sustainable level — combined with Week 4's break-even gap, this signals real unit-economics weakness, not a fundamentally broken idea. The available fixes are to raise the price (increasing both LTV and helping the earlier break-even problem at once), reduce churn through better onboarding (which increases LTV directly, since LTV is inversely related to churn rate), or find a cheaper acquisition channel (reducing CAC directly).
keyPoints: CAC = total spend ÷ new customers = ₦800,000 ÷ 40 = ₦20,000
LTV = monthly revenue ÷ churn rate = ₦1,500 ÷ 0.05 = ₦30,000
LTV:CAC = 1.5:1, below the healthy 3:1 benchmark
Fixes: raise price, reduce churn via onboarding, or find cheaper acquisition

theory.question: Explain why churn is called 'the other half of marketing,' using the worked churn example, and describe the two specific retention levers (onboarding and customer success) that address it.
theory.modelAnswer: Churn is called 'the other half of marketing' because acquiring new customers means little if existing customers are leaving just as fast — a venture spending heavily on acquisition while ignoring retention is effectively pouring water into a leaking bucket. This is made concrete in the worked example: at just 5% monthly churn, a venture starting with 200 customers in January would have only about 106 remaining by December if it acquired no new customers at all, meaning it would need to acquire roughly 94 new customers over the year purely to stand still, before any real growth. Two specific levers address this. Onboarding is the highest-leverage retention investment: it aims to minimise 'time to value,' the gap between a customer signing up and experiencing their first genuinely meaningful success, through an active, guided process rather than a passive welcome email or documentation page. Customer success is the second lever: proactively monitoring usage for early warning signs of churn, like declining activity or unused features, and intervening before the customer actually leaves rather than after — in an early-stage venture, this responsibility usually falls directly on the founders themselves.
keyPoints: Retention matters as much as acquisition — a 'leaking bucket' problem
Worked example: 5% monthly churn shrinks 200 customers to ~106 in a year
Onboarding: minimise 'time to value' through an active, guided process
Customer success: proactively watch for churn warning signs and intervene early
